claims.claim: A corporation is a business that exists as its own legal entity, separate from its owners; OpenStax's Introduction to Business defines a corporation as a legal entity that can own property, enter into contracts, sue and be sued, and engage in business operations under the terms of its charter, with a life separate from its owners.

Limited liability is the defining benefit of the corporate form: owners' liability for the corporation's obligations is limited to the amount they invested, and if the corporation goes bankrupt, creditors can look only to the corporation's assets for payment.

The corporate structure has three levels: stockholders (shareholders) own the corporation and elect the board; the board of directors governs the corporation, sets major goals and policies, and hires corporate officers; and officers (top management) run the corporation day to day, carrying out the goals and policies set by the board.

Advantages of the corporate form include limited liability, ease of transferring ownership (shareholders can sell their shares at any time without affecting the corporation), unlimited life, and the ability to attract financing by selling shares of stock.

Disadvantages of the corporate form include double taxation of profits (corporate profits taxed at the company level and dividends taxed again on shareholders' personal returns in the classic model), the cost and complexity of formation, and more government restrictions and reporting requirements than simpler business forms.
Corporations raise money by selling shares: dividing ownership into smaller units makes it affordable to more investors, and the money raised becomes capital for the business.

A public corporation's shares trade on open markets where anyone can buy them; a private corporation's shares are held by a small group and are not offered for sale to the public. The general distinction is supported by OpenStax (public corporations' shareholders can sell shares at any time; closely held firms are owned by a small group) and by SEC Investor.gov's description of public companies as those whose securities trade on public markets with regular public disclosure obligations.
Because the corporation is a separate entity, it has an independent life: the death, departure, or sale of an owner does not end the corporation.
Setting up a corporation is more complex and more expensive than starting a sole proprietorship or partnership, involving formation steps, fees, and ongoing reporting obligations.
Corporations range in size from large multinationals to midsize and small firms, and the corporate form is the dominant one for big business because of its ability to gather large amounts of capital.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether double taxation applies to all corporations
positions: OpenStax and the SBA describe double taxation of profits as a standard disadvantage of the classic corporate (C-corporation) model: corporate profits are taxed, and dividends are taxed again on shareholders' returns.
Some corporate forms in some jurisdictions (for example, S corporations in the United States) avoid double taxation, and tax treatment varies by jurisdiction and entity type.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names double taxation as a trade-off of the classic corporate model and states that tax treatment varies by jurisdiction; pass-through variants belong to sibling topics (llc, forms-of-business-ownership).

positions: Textbook sources state that owners are not personally liable for the corporation's debts and creditors can reach only corporate assets.
Owners remain personally responsible for their own misconduct and for debts they personally guaranteed; courts can also look past the corporate form in abuse cases.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the protection plainly for business debts and adds a one-line caveat that the shield does not cover personal wrongdoing or personally guaranteed loans.

positions: SEC Investor.gov (U.S. context): a company is public when its securities trade on public markets and it has public reporting and disclosure obligations.
General business-education usage: a public corporation is simply one whose shares are offered and traded openly; a private one keeps shares with a small group.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the simple general distinction (shares traded openly versus held privately) and avoids jurisdiction-specific reporting rules as universal claims.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate claims (for example, 'Corporation is a foundational concept in Introduction To Business' and 'College courses use corporation as a building block') state no verifiable facts about corporations and were discarded.
The draft's vocabulary definitions (for example, 'A foundational Introduction To Business concept covered in this lesson') are circular and were replaced with independently verifiable definitions.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generic draft with a source-verified lesson: attributed working definition (OpenStax), limited-liability example written fresh, three-level structure, named trade-offs, share-selling mechanism, and public-versus-private distinction.
Added the honest caveats that limited liability does not cover personal wrongdoing or personal guarantees and that corporate rules and taxation vary by jurisdiction.
Framed double taxation as a feature of the classic corporate model rather than a universal rule, per the subject source-map caution about jurisdiction-specific rules.

Supports: the working definition of a corporation as a legal entity with a life separate from its owners that can own property, contract, sue and be sued; the three-level structure (stockholders own and elect the board; the board governs and hires officers; officers run operations); advantages (limited liability, ease of transferring ownership, unlimited life, ability to attract financing by selling stock); disadvantages (double taxation, cost and complexity of formation, more government restrictions and reporting); and the public/closely-held distinction. Concepts adapted into original prose with attribution; no source sentences reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Choose a Business Structure (Corporation / C corp)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government guidance; U.S. context). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports the general corporate model only: a corporation is a legal entity separate from its owners that can make a profit, be taxed, and be held legally liable; owners get strong personal-liability protection; formation costs are higher and record-keeping, operational processes, and reporting are more extensive; corporate profits can be taxed twice (corporate tax plus dividends on personal returns); the corporation has an independent life separate from its shareholders; and corporations can raise funds through the sale of stock, suiting businesses that need capital or plan to go public. Jurisdiction-specific details were not stated as universal; all wording synthesized in original prose.
